papers.title: Study protocol for evidence-based LIFEstyle interventions for the delay of COgnitive DEcline among Singaporean older adults (LIFECODES): a randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Singapore's rapidly aging population has led to a widening gap between total and healthy life expectancy. Dementia affects approximately 10% of adults aged ≥ 60 years, and 152,000 people are projected to be living with dementia by 2030. Up to 45% of dementia cases may theoretically be prevented or delayed by addressing 14 modifiable risk factors across the life course. However, evidence on clinically effective, culturally tailored multidomain interventions for older Singaporeans remains limited. The LIFEstyle interventions for the delay of COgnitive DEcline among older Singaporean adults (LIFECODES) trial evaluates the effects of a multidomain lifestyle intervention on cognitive decline and the added value of individualized health coaching. Secondary aims examine epigenetic aging and systemic inflammation. LIFECODES is a three-arm proof-of-concept randomized controlled trial at the National University of Singapore (NUS) aiming to enroll 120 community-dwelling adults aged 60-75 years with signs of cognitive decline. Participants are randomized to group-based health education (GHE), GHE plus individualized health coaching (HC), or general care. The two-year intervention comprises 27 in-person sessions addressing eight lifestyle domains relevant to dementia risk: diet, physical activity, cognitive activity, social engagement, mental well-being, sleep, smoking and alcohol consumption. The primary outcome is cognitive processing speed. Secondary outcomes include memory, executive function and other cognitive domains, DNA methylation (DNAm) age, inflammatory biomarkers, functional status, psychosocial well-being, and sleep quality. As of 14 September 2026, 190 individuals had been screened, and 110 (57.9%) met the eligibility criteria. Seven eligible individuals withdrew before randomization and 12 withdrew after randomization. A total of 91 participants are currently enrolled in the study (GHE, n = 30; HC, n = 30; control, n = 31). The first rolling intervention cohort began on 15 May 2025. Among the 91 participants, the mean age is 68.7 years (SD 4.2), and 66 (72.5%) are female. Recruitment and follow-up remain ongoing. Interim recruitment and randomization indicate that a community-based multidomain dementia-prevention trial can be initiated in Singapore. Planned analyses will determine intervention efficacy and the added value of individualized health coaching for cognitive health and biological aging. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06661486, identifier NCT06661486.

papers.title: Associations Between Cannabis Use and Sleep Outcomes in a Sample of Pregnant Women.
papers.abstract: Both sleep difficulties and cannabis use during pregnancy (CUP) are common and associated with adverse birth and offspring outcomes. Sleep problems are a commonly reported motive for cannabis use during pregnancy. Estimate associations between cannabis use during pregnancy and common sleep difficulties across trimesters. This cohort study recruited pregnant women with lifetime cannabis use who used (n=298) and did not use (n=143) cannabis during pregnancy. Women who reported heavy episodic alcohol consumption or use of other illicit substances were excluded. Some women tested positive for cotinine in urine drug screens. Cannabis use was assessed at each trimester using self-report and urine drug screening. Presence of the nicotine metabolite, cotinine, was measured via urine drug screening at each trimester. Cannabis use during pregnancy (CUP) status was defined separately for each trimester as use versus no use and was treated as a time-varying exposure. The nicotine metabolite cotinine was included as a covariate in all models to account for nicotine exposure. Motivation for cannabis use during pregnancy was assessed during the first trimester. Insomnia symptoms (Women's Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale), daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale), subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index single item), and restless legs symptoms were assessed at each trimester. A CUP Status x Trimester interaction was observed for insomnia symptoms (F(2,737.81)=4.98, P FDR =0.03) wherein use during the third trimester was associated with heightened insomnia. Women reporting sleep difficulties as a motive for use reported worse insomnia symptoms (F(1, 223)=13.09, P FDR =0.001) and worse sleep quality (F(1, 219)=7.86, P FDR =0.01), relative to those using for other reasons. Elevated third trimester insomnia symptoms among pregnant women using cannabis compared to women who did not use cannabis suggest a potential trimester-sensitive association. Despite perceptions that cannabis improves sleep, women who reported sleep as their motive for CUP during the first trimester experienced greater insomnia symptoms and poorer sleep quality across pregnancy than those using cannabis for other reasons. Additional studies are needed to determine whether sleep-related difficulties precede cannabis use, follow it, are modified by it, or represent an epiphenomenon. Question: Is cannabis use during pregnancy associated with maternal sleep problems?Findings: Within this study of 441 pregnant women, cannabis use was associated with higher third trimester insomnia symptoms but not with other sleep outcomes. Women using cannabis to aid with sleep difficulties had worse insomnia symptoms and poorer sleep quality than those using for other reasons.Meaning: Cannabis use in late pregnancy may mark periods of greater insomnia symptom burden, suggesting that sleep problems during pregnancy may be an important clinical context for understanding cannabis use during pregnancy.

papers.title: Tyrosine hydroxylase deletion in Ntsr1 neurons confers resistance to diet-induced weight gain: an energy-balance analysis.
papers.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD) disrupts circadian feeding rhythms and promotes diet-induced obesity (DIO), but the neural mechanisms linking diet to energy balance remain unclear. Previously, we demonstrated that dopamine production in neurotensin receptor 1 ( Ntsr1 )-expressing neurons was required for HFD-induced daytime overfeeding and DIO. Here, we tested whether DIO resistance in Ntsr1 Cre ;Th flox conditional knockout (cKO) mice was explained by altered energy expenditure. We replicated resistance to HFD-induced weight gain and assessed food intake, indirect calorimetry, activity, body temperature, fecal energy, fecal nonesterified fatty acids, and the gut microbiome. Indirect calorimetry on standard chow diet (SCD) was confounded by reduced intake and body weight loss, whereas HFD-fed cKO mice consumed food readily and resisted weight gain. Unlike our previous study, daytime feeding was not suppressed; instead, cKO mice were slightly and variably hypophagic on HFD but not SCD. DIO resistance was not accompanied by increased energy expenditure, activity, or body temperature. Rather, cKO mice showed reduced energy expenditure and activity and lower body temperature on both diets. In the replication cohort, HFD fecal output was lower in cKO mice, whereas the independent bomb-calorimetry cohort showed no genotype difference in fecal mass; fecal energy density and nonesterified fatty acid concentration were unchanged. Preliminary analysis of the microbiome was consistent with an obesity-resistant gut profile. Together, these findings indicate that the feeding phenotype is diet- and experiment-dependent and that DIO resistance is not explained by increased energy expenditure, activity, thermogenesis, or detectable changes in fecal energy or fat content.

papers.title: Hypoxic Burden Predicts Symptomatic but Not Sleep Architecture Response to CPAP Therapy in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) remains the standard metric for assessing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity, although it does not fully capture the physiological consequences of respiratory events. Hypoxic burden (HB), which integrates the frequency, depth, and duration of oxygen desaturations, has been proposed as a more comprehensive measure of OSA-related hypoxic stress. This study compared the prognostic value of HB and AHI for subjective and objective treatment outcomes in patients undergoing continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy. Data from 412 patients with OSA who underwent diagnostic and CPAP-treated polysomnography were analyzed, including 52 patients with available follow-up questionnaires. HB was calculated using a validated event-based algorithm. Multivariable regression models were used to predict patient-reported outcomes and changes in sleep architecture, adjusted for age, sex and body mass index. HB consistently demonstrated stronger associations with symptomatic outcomes than AHI. Models including HB showed improved model fit and explained variance. HB remained independently associated with lower follow-up fatigue and better sleep quality after adjustment for AHI. In contrast, AHI was the dominant predictor of objective sleep architecture improvements, including increases in N3 sleep, reductions in N1 sleep, and reductions in arousal index. HB provided additional independent information only for changes in arousal burden. These findings suggest that HB and AHI capture complementary dimensions of OSA severity. While AHI primarily reflects sleep fragmentation and physiological response to CPAP, HB appears more closely related to subjective treatment benefit. Incorporating HB alongside AHI may improve clinical phenotyping and prediction of treatment response in OSA.

papers.title: Early Increases in Hippocampal Synchrony Predict Chronic Epileptiform Burden in a Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Model.
papers.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common focal epilepsy, is often drug-resistant and arises predominantly in the hippocampus. Disease severity is conventionally assessed by seizure frequency and duration, yet epileptiform activity outside discrete seizures may also track disease progression. Whether this activity reflects hippocampal network reorganization as part of epileptogenesis, and whether such reorganization predicts chronic severity, is unknown. Here, we combined longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of hippocampal CA1 neurons with repeated 24-hour EEG recordings that quantified epileptiform burden in the same pilocarpine-treated mice over 16 weeks. CA1 firing and synchrony rose acutely, subsided during a latent period, and increased again chronically, with synchronized firing organized into brief waves that propagated in a consistent direction. Epileptiform burden followed a similar temporal trajectory and increasingly contained electrographic seizures. CA1 synchrony correlated with epileptiform burden and stratified mice into groups with distinct neuronal and electrographic outcomes. CA1 synchrony measured within three weeks of pilocarpine induction predicted chronic epileptiform burden, identifying early hippocampal synchrony as a candidate imaging biomarker and pointing to an early window for intervention in TLE.

papers.title: Enhancing psychological wellbeing in STEM education through public health strategies across educational transitions.
papers.abstract: Student mental health is a growing public health concern in higher education, and small questionnaire datasets are often highly imbalanced and difficult to model reliably. This study empirically validates a Transition-Aware Public Health Wellbeing Network (TAPHW-Net) using an openly accessible questionnaire dataset and narrows the STEM-transition domain to the available variables. The source dataset contained 843 responses. Respondents aged 18-22 years were retained, and the analytic sample consisted of 777 students, classified based on the original survey label: No Stress (n = 38), Eustress (n = 710), and Distress (n = 29). 24 predictors were grouped into emotional/psychological, physical/somatic, academic pressure, social and environmental, and demographic branches. To prevent leakage of the targets, the direct recent-stress item was omitted. Median imputation, standardization, and SMOTE were applied in the training folds only. Five-fold out-of-fold evaluation was used to assess Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP, ANN, and TAPHW-Net. Logistic Regression had the highest fold-averaged accuracy (0.968 ± 0.019), macro-F1 (0.884 ± 0.048), and macro-AUC (0.996 ± 0.004). TAPHW-Net's pooled OOF accuracy, macro-F1 score, and macro-AUC were 0.8739, 0.6626, and 0.9523, respectively. It had lower overall accuracy, but it successfully retrieved 78.9% of the No Stress cases and 86.2% of the distress cases, although precision was only 0.385 and 0.397 for these two classes, respectively. Difficulty in the home environment, anxiety, palpitations, work-environment stress, sleep problems, and health problems were important predictors. The attention architecture did not outperform simpler models on this small and highly imbalanced tabular dataset. Its main value lies in domain-structured representations, minority-class recall, and transparent mapping of model importance to a hypothetical decision-support template. The findings are limited to the source dataset and require external validation before institutional use or transfer to STEM-specific and educational-transition settings.

papers.title: Norepinephrine inhibits Afferent activation of NTS Catecholamine Neurons in Mice.
papers.abstract: The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) integrates visceral sensory input to regulate feeding behavior, with catecholaminergic (CA) and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons playing key roles in energy homeostasis. Recent evidence suggests functional heterogeneity among CA-NTS neurons, including distinct subpopulations that either suppress or promote feeding. In this study, we investigated how norepinephrine (NE) modulates excitatory synaptic transmission from solitary tract (ST) afferents onto tyrosine hydroxylase-positive (TH⁺) NTS neurons in mice. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology in horizontal brainstem slices, we found that NE inhibits ST-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (ST-EPSCs) in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects at ≥10 µM and an EC₅₀ of ∼3.4 µM. This inhibition was mediated by α₂-adrenergic receptors and was independent of GABA A receptor activity. NE also suppressed asynchronous glutamate release and attenuated CCK-induced increase in spontaneous EPSC frequency, suggesting a presynaptic mechanism. NPY similarly reduced ST-EPSC amplitude via Y 2 receptor activation, and co-application of NE and NPY produce additive or synergistic effects, even at subthreshold concentrations. Together, our results reveal a novel mechanism by which noradrenergic and peptidergic systems interact to regulate visceral sensory processing in the brainstem. NTS.

papers.title: Circadian feeding rhythm loss drives sex-specific β-cell dysfunction in diet-induced obesity.
papers.abstract: Diet-induced obesity (DIO), modeled by a high-fat diet (HFD), adversely affects circadian glucose homeostasis partly by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles. However, its impact on circadian β-cell function and relevant transcriptional programs remains unclear. To investigate this, we exposed male and female C57BL/6 mice to either chow or HFD for eight weeks and assessed behavioral (feeding/activity), physiological (glucose tolerance/insulin secretion), transcriptomic (RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)), and epigenomic (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using Sequencing (ATAC-seq)) circadian rhythms. Additionally, we tested whether normalizing fasting/feeding cycles via time-restricted feeding (tRF) during the dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle could mitigate DIO's deleterious effects. DIO disrupted circadian fasting/feeding rhythms, with greater disruption in males than females (p<0.05 vs. CHOW). In males, DIO abolished circadian regulation of glucose tolerance and in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (p<0.05 vs. chow), whereas female mice maintained circadian glucose homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis of male islets revealed a 42.1% reduction in circadian-regulated transcripts under DIO, with weakened rhythms in key β-cell pathways such as insulin secretion. Moreover, ATAC-Seq analysis indicated reduced chromatin accessibility of genes/pathways related to insulin secretion and glucose hemostasis under DIO (p<0.05 vs. chow) during both dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle. Notably, dark-phase time-restricted feeding (tRF) restored circadian glucose tolerance, GSIS, and islet gene expression, whereas light-phase tRF enhanced β-cell function during the normally inactive/light phase of the circadian cycle, further suppressing circadian rhythmicity of the islet transcriptome. Motif analysis indicated that DIO suppressed the activity of D-box transcription factors (TFs) (DBP and TEF) while enhancing the activity of ETS family TFs (ELK1, ETS2, ELF2, and GABPA), which was partly mitigated by dark-phase tRF. Our study demonstrates that DIO disrupts circadian β-cell function and gene expression by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles in male mice and reveals significant sex differences in how DIO affects circadian glucose homeostasis and β-cell function.

papers.title: The relationship between Tai Chi exercise and psychological distress in older adults: the chain mediation effect of mood state and sleep quality.
papers.abstract: Psychological distress is a common mental health issue among older adults, significantly affecting their quality of life and overall health. As a traditional form of mind-body exercise, Tai Chi is gaining increasing attention for its mental health benefits. However, the effects of Tai Chi practice on psychological distress in older adults remain unclear, and the mechanisms underlying its impact on mood and sleep quality, in particular, still need to be explored. This study aims to explore the relationship between Tai Chi exercise and psychological distress in older adults, and to examine the chained mediating effects of mood state and sleep quality in this association. Questionnaires containing the Physical Activity Rating Scale (PARS-3), the Positive and Negative Mood States (POMS) scale, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQ), and the final versions of non-specific psychological distress scales (Kessler 10), a total of 457 valid questionnaires were collected. Analysis of the mediation effects in this study were statistically consistent with a mediating role of the relationship between Tai Chi exercise and psychological distress in older adults. The effect size of the total indirect effect was -0.265 (95% CI [-0.339, -0.197], p < 0.01), accounting for 53.9% of the total effect. The mediation effect consisted of three pathways. Path 1: Tai Chi exercise → Mood state → Psychological distress in older adults, with an effect size of -0.159 (95% CI [-0.221, -0.103], p < 0.01). Path 2: Tai Chi exercise → Sleep quality → Psychological distress in older adults, with an effect size of -0.067 (95% CI [-0.112, -0.032], p < 0.01). Path 3: Tai Chi exercise → Mood state → Sleep quality → Psychological distress in older adults, with an effect size of -0.039 (95% CI [-0.065, -0.020], p < 0.01). This study identified a significant association between Tai Chi exercise and the alleviation of psychological distress in older adults, and this association may be explained by the chained mediating effects of mood state and sleep quality.

papers.title: Partial agonists and heteromeric Kainate receptor desensitization.
papers.abstract: Kainate receptors (KARs) are glutamate-gated ion channels that mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. KARs assemble as homo- or heterotetramers composed of five subunits (GluK1-5), with heteromeric assemblies representing the predominant native population. Although KARs share overall structures and basic functional properties with other ionotropic glutamate receptor subfamilies, they exhibit distinct gating kinetics, particularly with respect to desensitization. While earlier studies have demonstrated how agonist binding drives gate opening and subsequent desensitization, the mechanisms governing partial agonism and desensitization of KARs, especially in heteromeric KARs, remain incompletely understood. Here, we combine electrophysiology and microscale thermophoresis binding assays to investigate how distinct KAR partial agonists control KAR desensitization and its recovery. While the onset rates of desensitization of homo- and heteromeric receptors activated by high/saturating concentrations of partial agonists are conserved between GluK2 and GluK2/GluK5 receptors, recovery from desensitization in heteromers is significantly slower than in homomers. Together with structural modeling and analysis of the GluK2 and GluK5 ligand binding domains (LBDs) in complex with orthosteric ligands, we show that agonist residence time and the extent of LBD bi-lobe closure across various agonists take precedence over subunit composition in governing KAR desensitization.

papers.title: Human herpesvirus 7-associated encephalitis diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing in pediatric patients: a retrospective study.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to describe the clinical features, treatment and prognosis of immunocompetent children with human herpes virus 7 (HHV-7)-associated encephalitis. Sixteen children with HHV-7-associated encephalitis were diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of their cerebrospinal fluid and followed up for 3 months. The median age of the cohort was 8.6 years (range, 1.4-11.8) and comprised of 8 males and 8 females. The most common presenting symptoms were fever (12/16, 75.0%), headache (10/16, 62.5%), and vomiting (8/16, 50.0%). Abnormal electroencephalography and encephalitis-related neuroimaging findings were obtained in 50.0% (6/12) and 25.0% (4/16) of the patients, respectively. 68.8% of the patients were treated with either acyclovir or ganciclovir. Unfavorable outcomes occurred in three patients, including the death of a 2-year-old child. Pediatric HHV-7-associated encephalitis generally has a favorable prognosis, but severe cases do occur. Early recognition is important for increasing clinicians' awareness of this condition.

papers.title: Intrinsic timekeeping in Escherichia coli.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks allow organisms to anticipate predictable environmental changes across the day-night cycle. Here we show that the bacterium Escherichia coli exhibits intrinsic timekeeping that anticipates daily temperature cycles. E. coli biofilms entrained to daily temperature shifts, producing 24-hour rhythms in curli plaque formation that persisted under constant temperature. Mechanistically, genetic analyses localized the autonomous timing machinery to the Rcs phosphorelay, which exhibits structural and conceptual parallels with other circadian systems. The BluFR sensory pathway, which acts upstream of the Rcs phosphorelay, linked temperature and blue-light cycles to rhythmic curli production. Flagellar promoter activity and curli production peaked at opposite times of day, suggesting daily coordination of adhesion and motility programs. These findings identify an intrinsic timing system in E. coli that expands our understanding of biological timekeeping.

papers.title: Practice patterns of midazolam administration in patients undergoing cardiac-related non-operating room procedures: analysis of a US anaesthesia database.
papers.abstract: Midazolam can be administered as an anxiolytic, a cardio-stable sedative, or an anaesthetic agent during non-operating room anaesthesia (NORA) procedures. Guidelines suggest avoidance in older or frail patients, and current practices are unknown. We hypothesised that there would be significant variation in midazolam administration for cardiac-related NORA procedures by attending and institutional characteristics, in addition to patient characteristics. This is a retrospective observational analysis of a multi-institution US-centric electronic health record dataset including all adult patients undergoing cardiac-related NORA procedures in the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group database from 2015 to 2022. The primary aim of the study was to identify the proportion of total variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient-, attending-, and institutional-level factors. The secondary aim was to identify practice pattern variations in the dosage and timing of midazolam administration. The primary outcome was any midazolam administration ≤1 h before anaesthesia start to 1 h after anaesthesia end. Secondary outcomes included total dose and timing of midazolam administration. Variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient, attending, and institutional factors was calculated with intraclass correlation coefficients following multilevel mixed-effects generalised linear models, in which a three-level nesting structure was assumed: patients nested within attendings and attendings nested within institutions. For the primary outcome, a binomial distribution and logit link function was specified. For the secondary outcome of total midazolam, the same three-level nesting structure was used, and covariates were modelled using a multilevel mixed-effects model specifying a Gaussian distribution and identity link function. A total of 246 918 cardiac-related NORA procedures with care provided by 5212 unique anaesthesia attendings across 63 institutions with a median case volume of 9 (inter-quartile range [IQR] 2-37) were included in the analysis. Midazolam was administered in 33.0% of patients (n=81 602), including 25.5% of patients aged ≥65 yr (n=40 469). Midazolam administration declined from 50.7% of patients in 2015 to 29.0% in 2022 (P<0.001). The median dose was 2 mg (IQR 2-2), with 89.9% administered before procedure start. For transoesophageal echocardiography procedures, it was estimated that 37.0% of midazolam administration (30.4-44.3) was attributable to attending variation and 26.4% (19.2-35.2) to the institution, assuming that 36.6% of the variation was attributable to known patient factors. For transcatheter/endovascular procedures, attending, institution, and patient factors accounted for 45.7% (39.0-52.6), 27.7% (19.7-37.4), and 26.6%, respectively. Although patient-level factors accounted for a meaningful proportion of variability, substantial variation in midazolam administration was also attributable to attending- and institution-level factors. Further studies on clinical outcomes and patient experience associated with this type of midazolam administration have the potential to inform future practice.

papers.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Molecular basis for allosteric regulation of RyR1 channel gating: effects of a therapeutic drug and oxidation-mimicking mutation.
papers.abstract: RyR1, an enormous, approximately 2.2 MDa, tetrameric calcium-release channel in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) of skeletal muscle, is essential for excitation-contraction coupling. Pathogenic mutations in RyR1 cause RyR1-related myopathies. ARM210 (S48168), a Rycal-class drug, has shown promise in treating RyR1-related myopathies in a recently concluded phase 1b clinical trial. Structural studies revealed that ARM210 binds to the peripheral RY1&2 domain of RyR1, stabilizing it in a closed state to prevent aberrant SR Ca 2+ leak. Here, we investigate ARM210's mechanism of action at the atomistic level using extensive all-atom (~2.5 million atoms) explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations totaling 36.6 μs. Simulations revealed a long-range allosteric pathway in the wild-type RyR1 that propagates over 200 Å, linking the RY1&2 domain to the pore-forming S6 helices of adjacent protomers and enabling pore opening. Subsequently, we demonstrated that ARM210 binding stabilizes the RY1&2 domain in a closed conformation, rigidifying the cytosolic shell and activation core and disrupting the allosteric network necessary for pore dilation. These findings describe a plausible mode of action for how ARM210 stabilizes RyR1 in a closed state by modulating long-range allostery. Furthermore, we show that this allosteric regulatory network is perturbed by the oxidative stress-mimicking C3892D mutation near the Ca 2+ activator site, identified via mass spectrometry, live-cell fluorescence microscopy, and electrophysiology.

papers.title: Systematic Spike Sorting Errors Revealed by Juxtacellular Ground Truth in the Awake Brain.
papers.abstract: Existing ground-truth data for spike sorting come almost entirely from anesthetized or in vitro preparations. Yet phenomena expected to challenge spike sorting most-spike overlap and bursting-depend on brain state and differ in the awake brain. Therefore, error estimates from existing benchmarks may not transfer to awake recordings, and the types of errors in the awake brain remain largely uncharacterized. To address this, we generated a ground-truth dataset (16 neurons) using paired juxtacellular-extracellular electrophysiology in awake mice, and found spike sorting performance, particularly recall, to be lower than conventional benchmarks might suggest. Generally, false negatives sharply increased with intrinsic physiological factors like bursting, whereas false positives were more strongly associated with extrinsic factors, such as putative spike overlaps. To quantify contributions to errors from intrinsic and extrinsic factors, for each observed juxtacellular waveform we predicted the corresponding extracellular waveform. In the best-performing sorter, we estimate approximately half of false positives were attributable to credulous attempts to resolve putative overlaps. Bursting and putative overlaps were each associated with a roughly doubled false negative rate when they occurred separately, and with a sevenfold increase when they occurred together. These co-occurrences accounted for approximately 40% of a typical neuron's false negatives, despite comprising only approximately a fifth of its spikes. Thus, the moments when spike sorters must rely on the assumption of waveform invariance the most to resolve overlaps are exactly the moments when bursting makes that assumption least valid. We also estimate that three-quarters of false negatives had been detected but assigned to other units. These spikes were not cleanly oversplit: post-hoc merging was not productive because the loss in precision was three times the gain in recall. Because bursting and spike overlaps often co-occur, sorting spikes by waveform similarity and repairing the result by post hoc merging is unlikely to adequately balance precision and recall in the situations of greatest scientific interest. That is, while bursting and spike overlaps may involve only a minority of spikes, the resulting sorting errors may disproportionately distort the interpretation of neuronal population dynamics. We thus conclude that uncertainty quantification in sorters' output is essential. Spike sorting, the assignment of extracellular spikes to individual neurons, underlies most large-scale recordings of brain activity, yet its accuracy has been validated almost entirely in simulations or in anesthetized or ex vivo preparations. Using simultaneous juxtacellular and extracellular recordings in awake mice, we show that conventional benchmarks likely overestimate sorting performance in the awake brain, and that sorting errors are highly structured. False negatives prominently concentrate where bursting coincides with spike overlap, and most appear to be detected but assigned to other, low-precision clusters, from which merging cannot cleanly recover them. Roughly half of false positives likely come from wrongly resolved spike overlaps. Because structured errors can masquerade as temporal relationships between neurons, they can disproportionately distort conclusions about neural coding, population dynamics, and functional connectivity. Our publicly available recordings provide a tool to devise more robust spike sorting assumptions, and our results argue for sorters that model burst-related waveform variability and report their uncertainty, especially during spike overlaps.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan -inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys.
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (∼60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (∼1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo . In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks.
papers.abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

papers.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control. Much of what we know about brain function comes from measuring how neural activity responds to specific events, from sensory stimuli and cognitive demands to targeted pulses of brain stimulation. Tracking these responses is fundamental for mapping how brain networks communicate in health and disease and for guiding interventions that modulate neural circuits. Because each response is buried in ongoing background activity and changes across repetitions, isolating it is difficult. Existing methods average repetitions inside short, hand-picked time windows, restricting researchers to seeing only the earliest, most stereotyped part of a response while leaving later, fluctuating activity invisible. Here, we introduce a new approach that combines the pattern-finding sensitivity of modern machine learning with the strict false-positive control of traditional statistics. Our method searches the period after each event without a preset window, using recordings of the brain at rest both to learn how a response differs from normal background activity and to measure what the model detects by chance alone. Using this tool, we show that human brain responses to electrical stimulation last over twice as long as previously recognized, revealing that brief perturbations trigger a longer cascade of neural activity than previously thought.

papers.title: False-Positive Calls of Reimplemented Published Analyses for Covert Command-Following on Electroencephalograms Recorded Without Study Commands.
papers.abstract: To measure how often published electroencephalographic analyses for covert command-following call patients positive without commands, and their detection of genuine responses. This cross-sectional study applied 11 reimplemented published analyses to electroencephalograms without commands: 974 clinical electroencephalography patients and, with rules fixed, 730 new patients; 38 with prolonged disorders of consciousness; and 544 comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Outcomes: false calls (share called positive) against a 5% benchmark, and genuine-response detection. Three of 10 command-following analyses called significantly more than 5% of clinical electroencephalography patients positive, replicated in new patients: Goldfine 2011, a spectral test, 23.3% (95% CI, 20.2%-26.6%), above its stated 5%; du Bois 2026, a criterion for entry to brain-computer interface training, 22.2% (95% CI, 19.2%-25.5%); and Guger 2018, a P300 accuracy threshold, 13.8% (95% CI, 11.5%-16.3%), near its approximate 12% chance rate (24.5% over 2 runs). The other 7 called 0.0% to 6.9%. After cardiac arrest: 11.5% to 27.3%. All 3 detected genuine responses. Identified contributors: a variance ignoring within-command dependence (Goldfine 2011), selection over configurations and times (du Bois 2026) and a permissive threshold (Guger 2018). Goldfine 2011's command-level correction, fixed before testing, called 0.8% of new patients and 2.4% after arrest, detecting 93.4% of stroke imagery-versus-rest sessions but few between imagery types. Reimplemented published analyses called up to 27% of patients positive without commands, more with repeated runs. A positive result needs its complete call rule's false-call rate and detection at that rate; imagery-versus-rest detection may reflect task engagement, not imagery.

papers.title: Increased variability in visual processing in children with autism.
papers.abstract: The visual evoked potential (VEP) indexes sensory processing, but the neurophysiological basis of altered VEP amplitudes in autism remains unclear. We examined whether reduced VEP amplitude reflects increased trial-to-trial neural variability and whether this variability relates to electrophysiological markers of cortical excitation/inhibition and developmental functioning. Pattern-reversal VEPs were analyzed in 102 typically developing (TD; 44 female) and 105 autistic (AUT; 15 female) children aged 2-12 years. N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes and inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) were computed. Resting-state periodic alpha activity and aperiodic exponent were derived using spectral parameterization. Associations among VEP, resting EEG, age, and developmental/behavioral measures were assessed using multiple linear regression. AUT children exhibited reduced N1 amplitude and lower ITPC, with marginally reduced N1-P1 amplitude. Higher ITPC was strongly associated with larger N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes, and group differences in VEP amplitudes were no longer significant after accounting for ITPC. Greater periodic alpha activity was associated with higher ITPC and larger N1-P1 amplitude, while a steeper aperiodic exponent was associated with higher ITPC in the pooled cohort. Within AUT children, higher ITPC was associated with better nonverbal development, verbal cognition, and language scores. Reduced VEP amplitudes in autism may primarily reflect increased trial-to-trial variability rather than systematically weaker stimulus-evoked responses. Associations between ITPC and resting EEG measures suggest that cortical excitation/inhibition may contribute to sensory response reliability. These findings identify neural response consistency as a developmentally relevant feature of visual processing in autism.

papers.title: Distinct Sex-Associated Phenotypes of Sudden Cardiac Arrest Across Clinical, ECG, and Echocardiographic Domains: Replication in Two Communities and Comparison with the Framingham Heart Study.
papers.abstract: Sex differences in sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) incidence and outcomes are well established, but risk stratification underperforms in women. It is important to delineate sex-specific patterns in SCA across clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic domains. We studied out-of-hospital SCA cases from the Oregon Sudden Unexpected Death Study (ORSUDS; Portland, 2002-2020; discovery) and Prediction of Sudden Death in Multi-Ethnic Communities (PRESTO; Ventura County, 2015-2024; external replication). Sex differences in 38 comorbidities, 19 ECG and 12 echocardiographic measures were estimated using multivariable-adjusted logistic regression. Female sex was the modeled dependent measure (male as reference). ORSUDS estimates were compared with those in the Framingham Heart Study (FHS), a community-based reference cohort, using FDR-adjusted Cochran Q tests. Among 5130 ORSUDS cases, 1715 (33.4%) were women (median age, 70.4 years [IQR, 58.7-81.8]) and 3415 (66.6%) were men (65.6 [55.0-76.8]). Compared with men, women had higher BMI (per 5 kg/m², 1.11 [1.08-1.15]) and higher odds of thyroid disease (2.56 [2.17-3.13]), asthma (2.33 [1.92-2.86]), mood disorder (2.17 [1.85-2.50]), dementia (1.27 [1.02-1.56]), and left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH, 3.13 [2.44-4.00]). Women also had lower odds of coronary artery disease (0.61 [0.52-0.71]), atrial fibrillation (0.67 [0.56-0.79]), prolonged QTc (0.45 [0.35-0.57]), prolonged PR (0.53 [0.41-0.68]), premature contractions (0.77 [0.60-0.98]), sleep apnea (0.53 [0.43-0.65]), and reduced LVEF (0.40 [0.29-0.54]). Most findings were replicated in PRESTO (n=2719). In contrast, several of these differences were reversed in the community (FHS, n=3539;FDR-significant): prolonged QTc was more common in women, whereas LVH, dementia, heart failure, and higher BMI were more common in men. Sex differences among SCA cases were mostly reproducible in SCA cohorts, and distinct from sex-related patterns in the community. These results have implications for development of sex-specific SCA risk assessment and prevention strategies. What is new?: This study is the first community-based analysis to comprehensively characterize pre-arrest sex-associated profiles across clinical, ECG, and echocardiographic domains, externally validate them, and compare them with a community reference population.Women with SCA were more strongly associated with non-cardiac comorbidities, LVH, preserved LVEF, and mitral valve abnormalities, whereas male cases were characterized by coronary and peripheral vascular disease, atrial fibrillation, prolonged PR and QTc intervals, premature contractions, and reduced LVEF.Several sex associations, including QTc prolongation, LVH, body mass index, heart failure, and dementia, differed in magnitude or direction from patterns in the community reference population.What are the clinical implications?: Our findings suggest candidate features for future sex specific risk factor analyses and potential components for sex-specific risk models for SCA.Clinicians may need to recognize the critical need to extend beyond dependence on just the value of the left ventricular ejection fraction for SCA risk prediction, especially in women.

papers.title: Sleep Irregularity and Risk of Incident Hypertension in the UK Biobank.
papers.abstract: Irregular sleep patterns are common and have been associated with higher cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of CVD, but evidence linking irregular sleep to hypertension is inconsistent. The objective of this study was to quantify associations between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. We conducted a prospective cohort study among 55,572 UK Biobank participants without hypertension or anti-hypertensive medication use who provided ≥5 valid days of accelerometry in 2013- 2015 (60% women, mean age 61 years). We measured sleep regularity using the intra-individual standard deviation (SD) of sleep duration and the sleep regularity index (SRI), a measure of the similarity of sleep-wake patterns from one day to the next. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for incident hypertension, identified through linked health records, by levels of sleep regularity adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors as well as employment schedule. We also evaluated differences by demographic, clinical, and sleep-related (defined by duration, efficiency, timing, and sleep disorders) subgroups, and interaction with genetic susceptibility to hypertension. During 7.9 years of follow-up, 5,713 participants developed hypertension. Participants with sleep duration SD >90 minutes had an 18% higher risk of incident hypertension compared to those with sleep duration SD ≤30 minutes (HR: 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06, 1.31). Similarly, participants in the lowest SRI quintile had a 40% higher risk than those in the highest SRI quintile (HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.52). These associations were generally consistent across demographic, health, and sleep-defined subgroups. Sleep irregularity and genetic susceptibility contributed independently to hypertension risk, without evidence of interaction. Irregular sleep patterns were associated with higher incident hypertension risk independent of established risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Maintaining regular sleep schedules may represent a modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention. What is new?: In this large prospective study using objectively measured sleep from wrist accelerometry, greater overall variability in sleep duration and more irregular day-to-day sleep-wake patterns were independently associated with higher risk of incident hypertension.Associations were robust to adjustment for potential confounding by demographic, socioeconomic, clinical, and lifestyle factors and were generally consistent across demographic, clinical, and sleep-defined subgroups.Sleep regularity and genetic susceptibility to hypertension were independently associated with hypertension risk, with no evidence that inherited risk modified the association between irregular sleep and incident hypertension.What are the clinical implications?: Maintaining consistent sleep schedules may represent an important modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention alongside established lifestyle recommendations.The association between irregular sleep and hypertension was observed regardless of genetic susceptibility, suggesting that improving sleep regularity may benefit individuals across the spectrum of inherited hypertension risk.These findings support future randomized clinical trials to determine whether interventions that improve sleep regularity can reduce blood pressure and prevent hypertension.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression.
papers.abstract: Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

papers.title: RyR2-Mediated Ca 2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca 2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca 2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent -verticilide for two months. RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca 2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca 2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca 2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca 2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: Spinal Noradrenergic Overdrive Promotes Reversible Motor Unit Aging and Sarcopenia.
papers.abstract: Sarcopenia is characterized by progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function with aging. Motor unit degeneration is a major contributor, but the mechanisms driving age-related deterioration of motor neurons, neuromuscular junctions (NMJs), and muscle fibers remain incompletely understood. Norepinephrine (NE) regulates spinal motor neuron excitability, but its role in motor unit aging has not been established. Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, optogenetics, fast-scan cyclic voltammetry, microdialysis, high-performance liquid chromatography, western blotting, and chemogenetics were used in mice aged 1-25 months. Motor neuron intrinsic properties were examined in 135 lumbar motor neurons from 81 mice. NE release dynamics, tissue content, and expression of the NE transporter (NET) and α2A-adrenergic autoreceptor were assessed in adult and aged mice. Descending spinally projecting noradrenergic neurons were selectively inhibited in aged mice using a retrograde chemogenetic approach. Aging produced progressive motor neuron hyperexcitability characterized by membrane depolarization, increased input resistance, elevated firing frequency, and altered action potential threshold (all P < 0.005). Optogenetically evoked endogenous NE increased motor neuron excitability by reducing action potential latency (P = 0.0001) and decreasing rheobase (P = 0.0028); these effects were prevented by α1-adrenergic receptor blockade (P = 0.0313). Aging enhanced stimulus-evoked spinal NE release, with greater responses at 20 Hz (P = 0.0223), 30 Hz (P = 0.0022), and 40 Hz (P < 0.0001). NE release elicited by stimulation of locus coeruleus and A5 noradrenergic inputs was also increased in aged mice (P = 0.0349 and P = 0.0016, respectively). Basal extracellular NE concentrations were unchanged, whereas spinal cord NE content increased (P = 0.0403). Aging reduced α2A-adrenergic receptor (P = 0.0009) and NET expression (P = 0.0046). Chemogenetic suppression of descending noradrenergic neurons in aged mice increased hindlimb muscle mass (P = 0.0111-0.0344), muscle fiber cross-sectional area (P = 0.0078-0.0467), NMJ innervation (P = 0.0210), and motor neuron soma size (P = 0.0353). Aging promotes spinal noradrenergic overdrive characterized by increased NE storage, enhanced activity-dependent NE release, and impaired autoregulatory control. Excessive noradrenergic signaling contributes to motor neuron hyperexcitability and motor unit deterioration. Suppression of descending noradrenergic activity reverses structural features of motor neuron, NMJ, and skeletal muscle aging, identifying spinal noradrenergic signaling as a potential therapeutic target for sarcopenia.

papers.title: Maternal separation remodels Purkinje cell circuits and impairs cerebellar synaptic plasticity.
papers.abstract: Early-life adversity has been associated with cerebellar abnormalities, but the cellular and circuit-level changes involved and their persistence across development remain poorly understood. We examined whether maternal separation (MS) disrupts cerebellar circuit maturation and whether these changes are accompanied by alterations in synaptic function and behavior. CD1 mice underwent daily maternal separation from postnatal day 2 to 18, whereas control litters remained undisturbed. Cerebellar alterations were assessed using transcriptomic and DNA methylation profiling, RT-qPCR, immunoblotting, Purkinje-cell morphometric analysis, and VGLUT1/VGLUT2 immunofluorescence. Patch-clamp electrophysiology was used to examine synaptic transmission and plasticity. Motor coordination, spontaneous locomotion, social approach, and stress-coping behavior were also evaluated. RNA sequencing of whole cerebellar tissue revealed early transcriptional remodeling, involving synaptic transmission, neuronal architecture, and plasticity-related pathways. Consistent with this profile, we found that MS altered Purkinje cell dendritic arborization and excitatory input remodeling, together with deficits in cerebellar long-term synaptic plasticity and reduced BDNF-related signaling. In parallel, methylation analysis revealed hypermethylation of the glucocorticoid receptor promoter and reduced cerebellar receptor expression, indicating that early-life stress also engages stress-related epigenetic mechanisms in this region. Importantly, these neurobiological changes were associated with motor coordination deficits, altered stress-coping behavior, and impaired social interaction. These findings identify the developing cerebellum as a target of early-life adversity and suggest that disrupted cerebellar maturation may contribute to lasting functional consequences. This study extends our understanding of the effects of maternal separation beyond the brain regions traditionally associated with stress responses.

papers.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Early and accurate identification of neurodegenerative disorders has notable implications for treatment and quality of life. Whereas neuroimaging-based biomarkers can accurately identify neurodegenerative subtypes, EEG represents a low-cost alternative that could expand access to dementia care. Here, we investigated whether six data-driven EEG latent factors, derived by nonnegative tensor decomposition of clinical EEGs, differ systematically across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative phenotypes. In 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET acquired within one year of each other, factor expression was compared across 14 diagnostic classes assigned by StateViewer, a validated artificial intelligence framework for FDG-PET interpretation. To separate disease-general severity from phenotype-specific topography, each factor was also regressed on a subject-level slowing index. Finally, we related the factors to regional FDG uptake and to neuropsychological performance (n = 98) and assessed their potential utility for single-subject classification. Four factors reflecting neurophysiological oscillations (posterior alpha, Rolandic beta, frontotemporal delta-theta and posterior theta-slow alpha) varied significantly across phenotypes, with attenuation of faster and augmentation of slower rhythms most pronounced in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), dysexecutive Alzheimer disease (AD) and posterior cortical atrophy, whereas factors dominated by eye-movement and muscle artifact showed no robust phenotypic association. Alpha and beta effects were largely attributable to overall slowing, whereas posterior theta-slow alpha became more phenotype-specific after adjustment (eta-squared 0.082 to 0.147), dissociating the Alzheimer disease spectrum from frontotemporal syndromes. The slowing index tracked with an FDG-PET pattern highly associated with DLB across the cohort, irrespective of assigned phenotype (r = 0.51, P < 0.001). Consistent with a model in which dementia phenotypes reflect altered hippocampal-neocortical oscillatory coupling (stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion), frontotemporal delta-theta tracked a limbocortical axis of metabolic pattern expression, rising with neocortical and falling with limbic-predominant involvement, independent of overall slowing and phenotype. Each factor mapped onto a distinct metabolic topography, with frontotemporal delta-theta resembling Alzheimer-type hypometabolism and posterior theta-slow alpha the medial occipital hypometabolism of DLB. In terms of neuropsychological performance, Rolandic beta was associated with executive functions, and frontotemporal delta-theta with memory, visuospatial and global performance. Using these four factors alone, an exploratory logistic regression classifier separated cognitively unimpaired participants from DLB, posterior cortical atrophy, typical AD, and dysexecutive AD (area under the curve > 0.8) but poorly discriminated frontotemporal dementia phenotypes canonically associated with 4-repeat tau. Thus, data-driven decomposition of clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artifact into factors that track metabolic phenotype, regional metabolism and cognition, capturing both overall slowing and phenotype-specific patterns. This work informs the further development of scalable, biology-informed EEG-based phenotyping of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning for infrared spectral analysis of bone.
papers.abstract: Infrared spectroscopy provides chemically specific information on bone composition, but conventional analysis often reduces spectra to predefined peak-ratio parameters. Here, we evaluated whether multivariate full-spectrum analysis improves bone phenotype classification. Optical photothermal infrared (O-PTIR) spectroscopy was used as the experimental IR modality, with wild-type (WT) and osteogenesis imperfecta mouse (OIM) bones representing typical and fragile bone phenotypes, respectively. Conventional parameters included mineral content, carbonate content, HPO4 content, mineral crystallinity, and collagen integrity. Classification using a combination of these parameters achieved 59-63% accuracy across partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) and machine-learning classifiers, whereas models using the 1800-800 cm-1 fingerprint region reached 87-90%. Models based on the collagen-rich region performed similarly to the full spectrum and better than the mineral-rich region. Similar performance across PLS-DA, logistic regression, and XGBoost showed that classification gains were driven primarily by spectral representation rather than model complexity. Variable importance in projection (VIP) and spectral-zone-based SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified prominent contributions from collagen-associated Amide I and II regions, with broader patterns of importance in PLS-DA and logistic regression and more localized attribution in XGBoost. Together, these findings support interpretable multivariate full-spectrum analysis as a complementary approach to conventional peak-ratio analysis of bone IR spectra.

papers.title: Pre-synaptic facilitation of corticospinal output improves dexterity and fine motor control after stroke.
papers.abstract: The corticospinal tract (CST) is a neural pathway that supports skilled use of the arm and hand. Lesions of corticospinal axons result in muscle weakness, deficits of gross motor function, and loss of proximal and distal dexterous control for which effective treatments are still lacking. Here we exploited excitatory connections from motor thalamus to primary motor cortex to potentiate surviving descending signals and restore volitional arm and hand control in three monkeys with corticospinal tract lesion, using deep brain stimulation. Stimulation targeted to thalamocortical projections facilitated upper-limb movements, enabling monkeys with arm and hand paralysis to perform unconstrained 3D reach and fine dexterous tasks. Stimulation improved strength, hand gross motor function, and digits control. Electrophysiology suggested that effects were mediated by and more effective when targeting fibers with monosynaptic connection to the corticospinal motoneurons. Stimulation was delivered in continuous with FDA-clinically approved parameters holding realistic promises of clinical translation.

papers.title: TALQ: A reproducible language model questionnaire for dense measurement of depressive and anxious states.
papers.abstract: Depression and anxiety are often assessed weeks or months apart with brief questionnaires covering few symptoms, leaving changes between assessments unobserved. Here, we introduce TALQ, a scoring system in which a large language model rates 52 symptoms from text, and use it to score 491 members of two online mental health communities every two weeks for a year. Ratings were stable across samples, predicted human annotations of interpersonal risk factors, low self-esteem and depression severity, and agreed with inventories completed by the same model. The scores mapped into 12 replicable symptom factors, including fearful preoccupation and social strain. Sleep disturbance and self-harm content consistently preceded overwhelm and emotional pain, respectively, two weeks later. People differed mainly in the states they occupied rather than transitions between them, and 13% entered in a crisis that remitted over months. Overall, our findings suggest that TALQ can measure expressed mental states densely and quantify longitudinal dynamics.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics.
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca 2+ ) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca 2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca 2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain.
papers.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

papers.title: Mice, marmosets and humans use ambiguous local motion to stabilize gaze.
papers.abstract: Animals need to infer properties of the environment that are only ambiguously encoded by neurons in the sensory periphery. Can these ambiguous signals drive behavior directly, or must the ambiguity first be resolved? We traced motion signals from the retina through the nucleus of the optic tract (NOT) to reflexive eye movements, combining retinal and in vivo electrophysiology, computational modelling, and eye tracking in mice, marmosets and humans. Using stimuli that dissociate local edge motion from global, object motion, we found that responses of NOT neurons were strongly biased towards local motion. This bias propagated to behavior: eye movements followed local motion; in mice, to the point that changing the edge orientation of vertically moving objects produced horizontal eye movements. Marmosets and humans exhibited similar biases, amplified in humans when central vision was masked. Thus, the brain can transform ambiguous sensory signals directly into behavior, without first resolving the ambiguity.

papers.title: Association between Sleep Quality and Perceived Oral Health among Adolescents: Analysis of the 2024 Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey.
papers.abstract: This study examined adolescent sleep satisfaction and its association with oral health. This study analyzed data from the 20th Youth Health Behavior Online Survey (2024), ultimately including 54,653 adolescents. Subjective oral symptoms were defined as tooth pain when consuming hot or cold foods or beverages, aching or throbbing tooth pain, and gum pain or bleeding within the past 12 months. Sleep-based fatigue recovery was assessed based on self-reported responses regarding the extent to which sleep during the past 7 days was sufficient to recover from fatigue. A complex sample design with weights, stratification, and clustering variables was used for analysis. Female students, high school students, adolescents with lower parental education, and those reporting lower subjective economic status and academic performance were more likely to report insufficient sleep-related recovery and to experience oral symptoms (p<0.05). Insufficient sleep-related recovery was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of experiencing oral symptoms (odds ratio=1.538; 95% confidence interval: 1.471∼1.608). Insufficient sleep is significantly associated with oral symptoms in adolescents. To improve oral health, interventions should address sleep-related breathing disorders and strengthen tobacco control strategies, while implementing programs to promote healthy sleep habits alongside existing oral health education.

papers.title: Oral Health-Related Functional Factors Associated with Different Levels of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Risk in Korean Adults: Analysis of a National Survey.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between oral health-related functional and symptomatic factors and risk of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) among Korean adults aged ≥40 years, with a focus on identifying oral health indicators associated with different levels of OSA risk. Data from the Eighth Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2019∼2021) were analyzed. Among 22,559 participants, 8,603 adults aged ≥40 years with complete data were included. OSA risk was assessed using a modified STOP-B28 questionnaire (Snoring, Tiredness, Observed apnea, high blood Pressure, and body mass index >28 kg/m2). Participants were categorized into normal, low-risk, and high-risk OSA groups, enabling a risk-stratified analysis. Associations between OSA risk levels and multiple oral health-related factors reflecting oral function and symptom history were examined using complex sample cross-tabulation and multivariable logistic regression analyses. Male sex was associated with a higher likelihood of belonging to the low-risk (odds ratio [OR]=1.244) and high-risk (OR=1.587) OSA groups than the normal group (p<0.05). Several oral health-related factors showed graded associations with increasing OSA risk. Individuals with masticatory discomfort had 1.349-fold and 1.595-fold higher odds of belonging to the low-risk and high-risk groups, respectively (p<0.05). In the high-risk group, moderate speaking discomfort (OR=1.482) and a history of toothache within the past year (OR=1.487) were independently associated with an elevated OSA risk (p<0.05). Oral health-related functional discomfort and symptom history were significantly associated with increasing OSA risk levels among middle-aged and older adults. By adopting a risk-based, stratified approach rather than focusing on diagnosed OSA or single oral symptoms, this study revealed that oral health indicators may serve as accessible markers for identifying individuals at elevated risk of OSA, underscoring the potential role of dental and oral healthcare settings in early screening and prevention.
